title: River Threshold
summary: A speculative civic threshold exploring movement, shade, and changing water conditions along the Mississippi River.
cover_image_alt: Abstract blue architectural study representing the River Threshold project.

gallery.alt: Primary concept rendering for River Threshold.
gallery.caption: Primary concept view exploring a layered public threshold at the river edge.

gallery.alt: Plan diagram showing the river edge, circulation bands, and program blocks.
gallery.caption: Site and circulation study.

gallery.alt: Section drawing showing stepped platforms and shade structures along the river edge.
gallery.caption: Section study focused on shade, movement, and changing water levels.

body:
## Project overview
River Threshold studies how a civic space can respond to the changing edge of the Mississippi River. The proposal treats circulation, shade, occupation, and water as parts of one adaptable public system rather than separate site elements.

## Design approach
The project develops a sequence of elevated and stepped spaces that move visitors between the city and the river. Large shaded zones create places to gather during hot weather while lower platforms allow the public realm to change as river conditions shift.

The design process focused on **movement, environmental response, and sectional experience**. Plan and section studies were used together to test how circulation could remain legible while the relationship between land and water changes over time.

## Key ideas
- Create a strong pedestrian connection between the city and river.
- Use shade as an architectural element rather than an afterthought.
- Allow portions of the public realm to adapt to changing water conditions.
- Build a sequence of spaces with different levels of enclosure and exposure.

title: Adaptive Courtyard
summary: A mixed-use courtyard study centered on passive cooling, daylight, and flexible community space.

body:
## Project overview
Adaptive Courtyard explores a mixed-use building organized around a shared environmental core. Rather than treating the courtyard as leftover open space, the proposal uses it as the primary device for daylight, passive cooling, circulation, and social activity.

## Environmental strategy
The surrounding program is arranged to maintain access to the courtyard while controlling direct solar exposure. Openings, shaded edges, vegetation, and circulation paths are coordinated to create a more comfortable microclimate and reduce dependence on fully conditioned interior circulation.

## Spatial goals
The project is intended to support both everyday use and changing community programs. Edges of the courtyard can shift between circulation, informal gathering, exhibition, and event space without changing the overall organization of the building.

## Key ideas
- Make passive environmental performance visible in the architecture.
- Use the courtyard as both infrastructure and social space.
- Bring daylight deeper into the building.
- Create flexible edges that can support multiple uses over time.

title: Material Commons
summary: A small-scale pavilion proposal testing repeatable assemblies and reclaimed material systems.

gallery.caption: Overall pavilion concept based on a repeatable structural rhythm.

body:
## Project overview
Material Commons is a small pavilion study centered on one question: how much spatial variety can be produced from a limited set of repeatable parts? The proposal uses a simple structural rhythm and reclaimed material panels to create an assembly that can be built, taken apart, repaired, and reconfigured.

## Fabrication logic
The system reduces the number of unique components so that fabrication can remain understandable and economical. Repeated connections are treated as a design opportunity, allowing the construction logic to become part of the visual identity of the pavilion.

## Material strategy
Reclaimed or surplus sheet material can be cut into a limited family of infill panels. Because the primary frame is independent from the panel system, damaged or changed pieces can be replaced without rebuilding the entire structure.

## Key ideas
- Reduce the number of unique fabricated parts.
- Make connections accessible and reversible.
- Design for repair, reuse, and changing configurations.
- Allow construction logic to contribute to the architectural expression.
